review_text:
This protocol describes the procedures for a randomized controlled trial of a play therapy programme for parents and their hospitalized under-5 children in rural India. The intervention provides child development guidance for parents along with interactive play sessions where parents can implement the tips they received, which has been shown to be an effective model for family learning and outcomes. Through families with young, hospitalized children in a rural setting, the study serves a population with significant healthcare needs and extensive opportunity for positive changes to cascade and increase many times over, including across the lifetimes of participating children and across families, with parents potentially sharing knowledge with other parents and putting it to use for other children. This is a valuable and thoughtfully designed study.

From my view, this promising study needs only a few revisions for clarification, detailed below in approximate order of appearance in the manuscript. In addition, I would like to note that the Statistical Methods section is not very specific, but this is not necessarily a problem as long as the analytical process is described in full for future publications. 
                The second primary objective, focused on parents (p. 6), is left out in parts of the text, including the Abstract, Statistical Methods, and Discussion. The Data Collection and Management section mentions home environment and parent-child interactions, but not the parent skills and knowledge described in the primary object. The HOME inventory arguably measures parenting skills, but if this is the goal, it should be made clearer.
                    The last two sentences of the first paragraph of the introduction (p. 4) need slight revision to make them understandable. I think “Play can also help learn how to adapt…” means to say “help children learn” or “help teach children” instead. I am not sure what this means: “Play and recreation mimic the therapy of allowing…” Maybe “Play and recreation are naturally therapeutic in that they allow…”?
                    Citation 16 (p. 5) is incorrect. It is attached to this statement: “Physical exercise, healing touch, music therapy, therapeutic massage, and health education have decreased cancer symptoms.” It is linked to “THE SINO-BRAZILIAN PRINCIPLES IN A LATIN AMERICAN” (References, p. 14), which is completely unrelated – it’s on legal frameworks, no mention of the relevant topics.
                    There are two secondary objectives (p. 6), but only one secondary outcome (p. 10). I recommend the authors either state why or add a clear outcome for the second secondary objective, like comparing effectiveness or satisfaction with online follow-up versus home visits.
                    Exclusion criteria on p. 6 state “Seriously sick, moribund children with life-threatening conditions.” Some discretion may be necessary, but this should be a bit more defined, if possible. Does the research team have an operational definition? (e.g., if the child is bedbound and/or highly immunologically compromised). If this is not possible, the team should track specific reasons children were excluded so that examples can be provided when non-identifiable (i.e., mentioning specific, extremely rare conditions would not be appropriate).
                    There is a typo on p. 8 – “Duration of the interventions”, point 2 says “monthly follow-up sessions. . .for one hour every week. . .” Everywhere but here says monthly, so I think “every week” just needs to be removed.
                    Although the timeline mentioned suggests that data collection may have already started, I am a bit concerned about the apparent inclusion of participants with infectious illnesses. It is good that the research team is requiring hand washing, but that does not seem sufficient to mitigate all risk, particularly with such young children, who are unlikely to have good hygiene practices. Therefore, I believe that the statement “There is no anticipated harm from the trial participation” (p. 8) and consent forms should mention that participation may increase the risk of infectious illness.

The second primary objective, focused on parents (p. 6), is left out in parts of the text, including the Abstract, Statistical Methods, and Discussion. The Data Collection and Management section mentions home environment and parent-child interactions, but not the parent skills and knowledge described in the primary object. The HOME inventory arguably measures parenting skills, but if this is the goal, it should be made clearer.

The last two sentences of the first paragraph of the introduction (p. 4) need slight revision to make them understandable. I think “Play can also help learn how to adapt…” means to say “help children learn” or “help teach children” instead. I am not sure what this means: “Play and recreation mimic the therapy of allowing…” Maybe “Play and recreation are naturally therapeutic in that they allow…”?

Citation 16 (p. 5) is incorrect. It is attached to this statement: “Physical exercise, healing touch, music therapy, therapeutic massage, and health education have decreased cancer symptoms.” It is linked to “THE SINO-BRAZILIAN PRINCIPLES IN A LATIN AMERICAN” (References, p. 14), which is completely unrelated – it’s on legal frameworks, no mention of the relevant topics.

There are two secondary objectives (p. 6), but only one secondary outcome (p. 10). I recommend the authors either state why or add a clear outcome for the second secondary objective, like comparing effectiveness or satisfaction with online follow-up versus home visits.

Exclusion criteria on p. 6 state “Seriously sick, moribund children with life-threatening conditions.” Some discretion may be necessary, but this should be a bit more defined, if possible. Does the research team have an operational definition? (e.g., if the child is bedbound and/or highly immunologically compromised). If this is not possible, the team should track specific reasons children were excluded so that examples can be provided when non-identifiable (i.e., mentioning specific, extremely rare conditions would not be appropriate).

There is a typo on p. 8 – “Duration of the interventions”, point 2 says “monthly follow-up sessions. . .for one hour every week. . .” Everywhere but here says monthly, so I think “every week” just needs to be removed.

Although the timeline mentioned suggests that data collection may have already started, I am a bit concerned about the apparent inclusion of participants with infectious illnesses. It is good that the research team is requiring hand washing, but that does not seem sufficient to mitigate all risk, particularly with such young children, who are unlikely to have good hygiene practices. Therefore, I believe that the statement “There is no anticipated harm from the trial participation” (p. 8) and consent forms should mention that participation may increase the risk of infectious illness.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard, however I have significant reservations, as outlined above.

This is an important article as it investigates the impact of a play intervention in a hospital setting. Previous studies have shown that long-term hospitalisation can lead to developmental losses, making this trial particularly timely, as few studies focus on this critical aspect. However, certain sections of the manuscript required clarification.

Firstly, the CONSORT diagram indicated that the trial had been completed (covering recruitment, refusal, intervention, loss to follow-up, etc.), but the text suggested that the trial was yet to begin. This discrepancy has since been addressed by the authors.

Secondly, it was important to clarify whether the intervention personnel would interact with the control group, as this could lead to contamination. The authors have confirmed that the intervention team will not be interacting with the control group. Additionally, the intervention was described as including nutrition and health components, raising the question of how these aspects would be distinguished from the developmental intervention involving play. The authors have clarified that the nutrition and health aspects will involve "sensitisation of parents during the hospital stay and home visits."

I would suggest that these sensitisation messages on nutrition and health be provided to the control group as well, ensuring that the play intervention remains the exclusive component in the intervention group. With the additional details regarding the intervention design and implementation, the manuscript now provides a clearer and more comprehensive account.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard.

I commend the authors for developing an excellent protocol for a scoping review on the effects of minor lower extremity amputations on balance impairments (primary focus) and interventions for postural control restoration (secondary focus). The need for this review has clearly been identified. The proposed methods have been refined through a detailed response to previous reviewer comments.

Additional considerations should be given to the outcome measures being collected. The authors plan to quantify balance impairments by collecting outcome data in two categories: patient-reported or performance-based.  Not all the outcome measures listed in the protocol have been validated in people with lower limb amputations (LLA).  Individuals with LLA have differing needs and capabilities. It is recommended that the authors consult a systematic review which identified outcome measures that have psychometrically validated for LLA populations (1). The authors can then report their findings in terms of outcome measures validated for the LLA population and those outcome measures that are used in other patient populations. Further, outcomes measures that demonstrate health related quality of life improvements should also be added to this scoping review.

This systematic review offers a significant contribution to understanding the efficacy of treadmill training in enhancing balance and reducing fall risk among older adults. The methodology encompasses a comprehensive literature search and analysis of approximately fifteen studies evaluating various treadmill training protocols. The findings suggest potential benefits for improving balance and mobility, particularly for individuals with Parkinson's disease or spinal cord injuries. The conclusions appear largely substantiated by the presented evidence, and the acknowledgment of limitations is appropriate. The authors rightly emphasize the significance of synthesizing disparate research. A recommendation for further investigation to optimize training protocols and address individualized needs is critical. However, several aspects warrant further consideration to enhance the review's clarity, rigor, and practical applicability.

Methodological Clarity and Transparency: An inconsistency in the reported number of included studies (n=16 in the abstract versus n=15 in Table 1) warrants attention regarding transparency. The authors should explicitly state the final number of studies included within the results section and reconcile this discrepancy through verification and subsequent updates to both sections.

Data Interpretation and Contextualization: Regarding Table 1: study by Hesse et al., 1997, updating the 'Study Type' field to 'Quasi-experimental study' is recommended if methodologically accurate. Furthermore, contextualizing the findings in relation to existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses would significantly enrich the review by providing a broader scholarly perspective and identifying areas of convergence or divergence.

Methodological Rigor and Bias Assessment: Explicit reporting of blinding procedures within the included studies is necessary to facilitate a robust assessment of potential bias. Acknowledging limitations arising from the absence or non-reporting of blinding procedures is also crucial for a comprehensive evaluation of study quality.

Please carefully review Table 1's columns and consider these revisions for clarity and conciseness:

Change "Paper Title" to "Author(s), Year" without the title for easier reference and table management.

Change "Study Type" to the more precise "Study Design."

Revise "Population Characteristics" to "Participant Characteristics" and add an "Age" field for comprehensive participant details.

Add a "Country/Setting" column to provide important contextual information, if possible.

Combine "Intervention" and "Duration" into a single column for better readability (e.g., "Treadmill training, 8 weeks").

Add separate columns for "Primary Outcome(s)" and "Secondary Outcome(s)" of the studies.

Include a column specifying the "Outcome Measurement Tools" used for each outcome.

Furthermore, concerning citation analysis within Table 1, if a literature review is cited, it is essential to examine the original primary studies referenced within that review and include those primary studies in the systematic review if they meet the pre-defined inclusion criteria.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard, however I have significant reservations, as outlined above.

In this manuscript Landherr et al compare the effect of the common SARS-CoV-2 ORF3a Q57H mutation to the parental sequence on host cells using ectopic over expression strategies.  The manuscript presents the interesting finding that over expression of the ORF3a Q57H protein decreases apoptosis relative to that observed by the parental protein, and that this difference is due to greater activation of the extrinsic apoptosis pathway by the parental protein.  These data are the strength of the manuscript.  However, there are several critical issues not adequately explained or addressed.  Below are specific comments and suggestions to improve the manuscript.

Specific Comments

1. Differences in ORF3a Protein Expression:

-The expression strategy employed is somewhat unusual, in creating an ORF3a-p2A-GFP fusion construct in which the primary translation product undergoes efficient self-cleavage mediated by its picornavirus p2A protease domain, liberating GFP and ORF3a-p2A polypeptides.  This allows tracking transfected cells by GFP fluorescence and the comparison of ORF3a-p2A expression between variant and parental proteins indirectly by performing immunoblots for GFP and quantitating the amount of the fusion proteins and liberated GFP.  They report that, contrary to a computational prediction by Wang et al that the Q57H variant will be less stable than the parental protein, that it is somewhat more stable.  A weakness of this approach is it ignores the possibility that the p2A-GFP fusion to ORF3a has a stabilizing effect on the fusion protein.  Furthermore, by utilizing immunoblots to GFP it makes the assumption that liberated ORF3a-p2A peptides from parental and Q57H variants degrade at equivalent rates and that GFP immunoblots reflect the amount of ORF3a-p2A protein.  It would have strengthened the paper to have directly measured the relative amounts of ORF3a-p2A protein with an anti-ORF3a antibody.

-The statement "Differences in protein expression levels between WT and mutant ORF3a are more likely to occur via post translational processes rather than transcriptional regulation" (Results, Paragraph 1).   It is not clear what the relevance of transcriptional regulation in transfected cells is when expression of the ORF3a mRNA is regulated quite differently in the context of SARS-CoV-2 infected cells than in transfected cells. Even in the context of transfected cells this claim would need experimental evidence, such as qRT-PCR for transcriptional analysis, post-translational modification studies, or protein folding studies.

2. Differing Results From Previous Studies:

-The results negative related to ORF3a effects on inflammasome activation, ER stress, and autophagy in this paper differ from other reported studies.  The authors should discuss potential reasons for these discrepancies.  One obvious difference regarding inflammasome activation is the use of H9c2 cells, a cardiomyoblast cell line, in the current work.  It is likely that these cells are not competent for inflammasome activation since Figure 3A shows that pharmacologic activation of inflammasomes by Nigericin fails to activate inflammasomes (IL-beta or caspase-1 cleavage) in these cells.

3. Mechanistic Studies on Q57H Mutation:

-The manuscript lacks detailed mechanistic studies on how the Q57H mutation could affect extrinsic apoptosis pathway activation.  For example, the authors should have examined the effect of individual death receptor knockdown on ORF3a induction of the extrinsic pathway for apoptosis to both identify the receptor activated and confirm their results.  Additionally, the authors should investigate and discuss the potential alterations in ORF3a interaction with death receptors, and any differences in downstream signaling activation between WT and Q57H. Comparative studies between WT and Q57H regarding their interactions and signaling pathways would significantly enhance the manuscript's contribution to the field.

Conclusion:

The manuscript presents interesting findings but requires substantial improvements in experimental support and detailed mechanistic studies. Addressing the points mentioned above will strengthen the manuscript and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the ORF3a protein's role and its mutations.

We confirm that we have read this submission and believe that we have an appropriate level of expertise to state that we do not consider it to be of an acceptable scientific standard, for reasons outlined above.

This brief report articulates views on the state of narrative CVs that were collected from a workshop and survey; while the authors recognize that the limited number and fairly narrow composition of these views might over-index on some items while underplaying others, they posit (and I agree) that this efforts like these are valuable in identifying areas for further inquiry to ensure that narrative CVs can be more effectively employed in assessing research and researchers.

The points raised are well-taken and provide a good landscape of many issues facing uptake, use, and potential issues with the narrative CV format, which holds promise as a way to reduce reliance on traditional quantifiable metrics, but also introduces the potential for new challenges and barriers to adoption.

Within the report, the wide variety of insights and observations raised by the authors are all relevant and interesting but feel a bit unstructured in some places and redundant in others. This makes it harder than necessary to walk away with a cohesive view on the themes raised. My main recommendation, therefore, is primarily oriented toward clarifying dominant themes within (or across) the major sections such that a reader can more easily digest the useful content.

For example, the 
                Views on narrative CVs/challenges with their usesection represents many findings that are each individually interesting, but which might be largely clustered into four major themes: narrative CV’s potential to engage an increased diversity of people and backgrounds; the need to balance flexibility and structure; the potential for bias on the part of both researchers and assessors; and headwinds that might discourage uptake. Stating these themes before introducing the more detailed findings will help a reader first grasp higher-level principles, which can then be expounded upon with the more concrete findings.

Similarly, 
                Changes as a result of introducing narrative CVs seems to center on three main ideas: the potential for unexpected positives; the need for support/training for both researchers and assessors; and the need to collect/evaluate implications and value that arise from use. 
                Expectations for the futurecenters primarily on seeing NCVs as an iterative, collective effort — top-down and bottom up, with diverse views and trajectories — if it is to yield collective benefits. Finally, the 
                Discussion summarizes five main prongs, some of which pull from sections above: possible (unexpected) benefits of CVs; the need for thoughtful support and communication to avoid amplifying known inequities or creating new ones; areas for further research and analysis; the need for open, diverse,  and continual communication; and recognizing that narrative CVs require a systems approach.

In each of these sections, the addition of even a single sentence stating these kinds of overriding themes (with possible minor reorganization of a point here or there) would increase the chances that a reader comes away with a more coherent sense of the major issues and possibilities, and — perhaps more importantly — can help make those findings ‘stickier’ and more memorable such that they take these very useful insights forward into other conversations and activities in the responsible research assessment space.
